The private bus to the Kuttanad school stopped at every jetty, and by the third stop the back seats had started. "Fish girl," Binoy said when Anjali climbed in, and two boys held their noses. Anjali's father ran the fish stall near the ferry.
Elizabeth had the window seat. She knew Anjali from Sunday class. She pressed her forehead to the glass and watched the paddy fields slide by. I'm not the one saying it, she told herself. If I open my mouth, they'll start on me.
Anjali sat in front of her, very straight, holding her bag on her lap. She got off one stop early and walked the rest of the way in the heat.
The next morning Anjali wasn't on the bus. Elizabeth kept looking at the empty seat in front of her.

qa.q: What did Binoy call Anjali when she climbed in?
qa.a: Binoy called her "Fish girl", and two boys held their noses.

qa.q: Why did staying quiet feel safer to Elizabeth?
qa.a: She told herself she wasn't the one saying it, so she felt less to blame, and she worried the boys would start on her if she spoke.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth realistically do the next time this happens?
qa.a: She could sit beside Anjali, say a short "Leave it" to the boys, or tell a teacher; even talking to Anjali afterwards would show her she isn't alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Anjali when nobody on the bus says anything?
qa.a: It likely feels as if everyone agrees with the boys; she sits very straight, gets off early, and the next day she avoids the bus altogether.

grounding: It shows a teenager staying silent while a classmate is teased, feeling less responsible than the teaser, while the harm still happens.

passage:
In Grade 9 Life Orientation at a school in Durban, groups of four were making a poster on saving water. Sami had moved from Cairo in March, and when he read out his part, Thabo copied his accent in a squeaky voice. The others laughed. Sami stopped reading and pushed the paper across to Lindiwe.
Lindiwe didn't laugh. She kept colouring the tap on the poster very carefully, staying inside the lines. It's not me doing it, she thought. He'll be fine, it's only a joke.
When the bell rang Sami packed up fast. At lunch Lindiwe saw him eating alone by the netball court, earphones in, facing the fence. She walked past with her friends and felt her stomach turn.

qa.q: What were the groups making in Life Orientation?
qa.a: The groups of four were making a poster on saving water.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe's careful colouring suggest about what she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was uneasy and trying to stay out of it; telling herself it wasn't her doing and only a joke made silence feel acceptable.

qa.q: What small step could Lindiwe take to make things better?
qa.a: She could sit with Sami at lunch or ask him to finish reading his part, and next time say "Let him finish" when someone mocks him.

qa.q: How might Sami see Lindiwe's silence?
qa.a: Sami might count her among the people who didn't care, since nobody stopped the mocking; eating alone facing the fence shows how shut out he felt.

grounding: It shows a teenager who stays silent while a classmate is mocked, feeling less responsible than the mocker, though the classmate is still hurt.

The physics batch at the coaching centre was fifty students under humming tube lights. Farhan went up to solve the pulley problem and got the direction of tension wrong. From the third row someone said, "Topper ji," and the laughter rolled forward. The sir smiled and moved on.
Ganga knew the right answer, and she knew Farhan's mistake was a common one. She almost said so. Then she thought, I didn't laugh. That's enough. And if I stand up for him, they'll tease me next.
After that week Farhan stopped coming to the board. He sat at the back and copied solutions without a word. Ganga noticed his hand never went up again, not even for questions she was sure he knew.

qa.q: Which problem did Farhan get wrong at the board?
qa.a: Farhan got the direction of tension wrong in the pulley problem.

qa.q: Why did Ganga think not laughing was enough?
qa.a: Not joining in made her feel she had no part in the teasing, and she was worried that standing up for Farhan would make her the next target.

qa.q: What could Ganga have said that fit the classroom?
qa.a: She could have said aloud that it's a common mistake, or asked for the tension direction to be explained, which turns attention back to the physics and away from Farhan.

qa.q: What changed for Farhan after that week?
qa.a: He stopped coming to the board and sat at the back copying solutions; the laughter cost him the confidence to answer at all.

grounding: It shows a teenager who watches a classmate being teased and stays silent, feeling less responsible than the teasers, while the classmate withdraws.

Dear Jahnavi Didi,
Something's been bothering me, and you always tell me the truth.
In our class, Mohit has a patched school bag, and Varun's gang has started calling him "Tailor-ji". Every morning in the assembly line they pass it down, whisper by whisper. I stand two places behind Mohit. I never say anything. I tell myself I'm not the one saying it, so it isn't really on me. And if I spoke up, they'd start on me next.
Today Mohit didn't come to school. His bench looked strange, empty. Our class teacher asked if anyone knew why, and I looked at my shoes.
I didn't tease him. So why do I feel like I did?
Write back soon,
Akash

qa.a: They call him "Tailor-ji".

qa.q: Why does staying silent feel safer to Akash than speaking up?
qa.a: Akash isn't the one saying the name, so it feels like someone else's fault, and speaking up might make the gang turn on Akash next.

qa.a: Akash could stand beside Mohit in the line, refuse to pass the name along, and tell the class teacher or the school counsellor what has been happening.

qa.q: What might those mornings in the assembly line be like for Mohit?
qa.a: He hears the name passed down every day and sees nobody stop it, so he may feel alone and dread coming to school.

grounding: A teenager who watches a classmate being teased every day stays silent, feeling less responsible than the teasers even as the harm grows.

passage: Suraj, you know Anisha from our tuition batch? Last month, in the online class, her camera came on by mistake. Her little brother was crying behind her and the wall had a big damp patch. In the side chat, Rakesh typed "haunted house tour" and people sent laughing faces. I saw every message. I didn't type anything, not even one emoji. I told myself, I'm not Rakesh, I'm just reading. But Anisha saw the chat too, when the teacher shared the screen later by accident. She switched her camera off and never turned it on again. Last week she moved to another batch. Twenty people were in that chat, and not one typed "stop". I was one of those twenty. I'm Naveen, not Rakesh. I'm just not sure that matters anymore.

qa.a: Rakesh typed "haunted house tour".

qa.q: How does Naveen feel now about staying silent in the chat?
qa.a: Naveen feels guilty and uncertain, admitting to being one of the twenty who never typed "stop" and not being sure being different from Rakesh matters anymore.

qa.q: At what moment could Naveen have changed things, and what could Naveen do now?
qa.a: Typing "stop" when the jokes started might have helped; now Naveen could message Anisha to say sorry and tell the tuition teacher what happened.

qa.q: How might Anisha have felt when she saw the chat?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and alone, seeing twenty classmates watch a joke about her home and none of them object.

passage: On the late bus back from the inter-school quiz, the seniors at the back started on Mohit again. "Say 'vegetable' again, Mohit! Vej-i-table!" Laughter. Mohit, new from Kerala, stared out of the window, ears red. Imran sat two seats ahead with the quiz trophy on his lap. He could have turned round. He could have said, "Enough." Instead he put his earphones in and told himself: I'm not the one saying it. It's not my joke. The bus was loud, the ride was long, and there was a maths test the next day anyway. When they got off, Mohit walked home fast without saying goodbye. Imran lay awake that night replaying the red ears. Not saying anything hadn't stopped a single word. At 7 a.m. he went to the staffroom and told Mrs D'Souza what he had seen. She thanked him and called Mohit in before first period.

qa.q: Why did Imran put his earphones in instead of speaking up?
qa.a: Imran felt awkward and less responsible because he wasn't the one saying it, so staying silent felt safer and more innocent than stepping in.

qa.a: He told Mrs D'Souza the next morning; next time he could say 'Enough' or sit with Mohit, and tell a teacher the same day.

passage: In the Class 10 group chat, someone posted a photo of Kalyani's cracked old phone with the caption "museum piece". Laughing faces poured in. Anand, lying on his bed in their Pune flat, saw it all. He didn't laugh. He didn't add anything. He also didn't write "not cool". Not my joke, he thought, and scrolled on. The next morning Kalyani wasn't in class. Her best friend said she had cried all evening and didn't want to come. Anand felt sick. If he had posted the photo himself, he'd know he was guilty. But he had only watched, and somehow that had let him feel clean. At lunch he went to their class teacher, Mr Kulkarni, and showed him the chat. Mr Kulkarni thanked him, spoke to the class that afternoon, and phoned Kalyani's parents before the day ended.

qa.a: The caption was 'museum piece'.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel 'clean' after the chat?
qa.a: Anand felt less guilty because he hadn't posted or laughed; watching silently seemed innocent, until Kalyani's absence made him feel sick.

qa.a: He showed the chat to Mr Kulkarni, who spoke to the class and phoned Kalyani's parents that day, so an adult could stop the harm.

qa.a: Kalyani felt humiliated and hurt, crying all evening and staying home the next day.

"They did it again today. The cricket-shoe thing."
Vinita looked up from her homework. "To Dev?"
"Yeah. Rohit hid his shoes, and everyone laughed when he had to field in socks."
"And you?"
"I didn't do anything."
"That's what I'm asking."
Siddharth shrugged. "I didn't hide them. I didn't laugh. I'm not the problem."
"Dev still played in socks."
"So I'm supposed to fight Rohit?"
"You're supposed to stop pretending doing nothing is nothing." She put her pen down. "Mumma! Come here a second."
Their mother came in, drying her hands. Siddharth told her, slowly. She listened, then picked up her phone. "I'm messaging Dev's class teacher now. And tomorrow you sit with Dev at lunch." Within minutes the teacher replied: "Thank you. I'll speak to the boys first thing and check on Dev." Siddharth nodded, oddly relieved.

qa.q: What did Rohit hide?
qa.a: Rohit hid Dev's cricket shoes.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth say 'I'm not the problem'?
qa.a: Siddharth feels defensive and less responsible because he didn't hide the shoes or laugh, so doing nothing feels innocent.

qa.q: What happened that evening, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Siddharth told their mother, who messaged Dev's class teacher, and he agreed to sit with Dev at lunch, so the teasing gets stopped and Dev isn't alone.

qa.q: How did Vinita see Siddharth's silence?
qa.a: Vinita saw that doing nothing still left Dev fielding in socks, and refused to let it count as nothing.

It happened in the canteen last term. A few boys kept calling Harsha "Tiffin Box" because his mum packed him big steel dabbas every day. They made the clanging sound whenever he opened one.

I was at the next table. I laughed once, then stopped, and after that I just ate. I remember thinking, I'm not the one saying it. I'm only sitting here. It felt safer to look at my plate than to say anything and have them turn on me.

Harsha started eating in the library corridor. By Diwali he'd stopped bringing the dabbas.

I'm Nikita. I still think about how I told myself I was neutral. There's no neutral table in a canteen.

qa.a: They kept calling Harsha "Tiffin Box".

qa.q: Why did looking at the plate feel reasonable to Nikita at the time?

passage:
Class teacher's note, Grade 9B, Friday.

During the group project break, I saw Jaya's classmates mimicking her stammer while she read her part aloud. Pooja, who sits next to Jaya and is usually kind, kept her head down and underlined her textbook very hard. When I asked Pooja later, she said, "I didn't say anything to her, ma'am. I wasn't part of it." She sounded relieved to say it, then her eyes filled.

Jaya went quiet for the rest of the day.

What I did: I spoke to the students who mimicked Jaya before the last bell and informed the school counsellor the same afternoon. I also sat with Jaya, told her it was not her fault, and called her mother. On Monday I will talk to the class about what standing by means.

qa.q: What were Jaya's classmates doing while she read aloud?
qa.a: They were mimicking her stammer while she read her part aloud.

qa.q: Why did Pooja seem relieved to say "I wasn't part of it"?
qa.a: Staying silent felt less blameworthy to Pooja than joining in, so saying it eased her guilt for a moment, though her tears show she still felt bad.

qa.q: What could Pooja do the next time something similar happens?
qa.a: She could sit closer to Jaya, say one short line to stop it, or tell the teacher straight away.

qa.q: How did Jaya seem to be affected by what happened?
qa.a: Jaya went quiet for the rest of the day, suggesting she felt hurt and embarrassed.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager who stays silent while a classmate is teased and feels less responsible, while the classmate is still hurt.

Wednesday night

Today in PT, Karan and his lot started calling Preeti "the elephant" when she was running. Everyone laughed. I didn't. I just tied my shoelace for about five minutes.

On the bus I kept telling myself: you didn't say it, Yogesh, so it's not on you. Karan's the mean one. And if I'd said something, they'd have started on me. That makes sense, right?

Except Preeti sat alone on the bus and didn't even take out her phone. She just looked out of the window.

Not laughing isn't the same as helping. I know that. Tomorrow I'm sitting next to her at lunch. And if it happens again, I'm telling Coach.

On the school bus from the market to the kasba school, the back-seat boys had found a new game: making Madhav say "Parliament" and laughing at his stammer. Every day he tried, and every day they laughed louder.
Rehana sat three rows in front. She never laughed. She also never turned round. It's not me doing it, she told herself. I'm just sitting here.
On Friday Madhav got off the bus two stops early and walked the rest of the way in the heat, alone.
That evening Rehana couldn't eat. "I didn't do anything," she told her mother. "That's the problem, isn't it? I didn't do anything."
Her mother put down the ladle. "Tell me all of it." She listened, then called the class teacher that same evening. By Saturday morning the teacher had spoken to the driver and the boys' parents, and Madhav had a seat at the front, next to Rehana.

Deepika sat two steps above. She saw Jaya's ears turn red, saw her reach for the shoe and miss. Deepika's own throat felt tight. Say something, she thought. But Karan was loud, and it wasn't her he was teasing. She looked down at her phone.
